archetype.name: Rebuilding (offense ahead of defense)
archetype.definition: A Saints team whose passing game can move the ball, but whose giveaways and a defense that has fallen from top-10 to bottom-six by EPA have it playing like the bottom third of the league.

report.headline: Turnovers and a collapsed run defense sink a passing game that can function
report.take:
New Orleans is 1-4 with a -6.6 point differential, and the efficiency agrees with the record. Net EPA ranks 27th, which is right where a 1-4 team usually lives. The -1.09 wins below expectation says they've been a little unlucky, not that a good team is hiding in there. Since 2023 the franchise has slid from a 9-win, top-7 net EPA team to back-to-back 5- and 6-win seasons. This year continues that slide rather than breaking from it.

The offense is better than its rank of 23rd suggests. Tyler Shough has started every game, and the team averages 23.6 points, 16th in the league. When he plays clean the passing game has real juice: 410 yards at Detroit and +10.9 pass EPA in the upset at Baltimore. The problem is the ball. Eleven giveaways in five games (3, 0, 4, 1, 3) have produced a -1.2 turnover margin per game, 30th in the league. The Vikings game showed the floor: 96 passing yards and -11.9 pass EPA against the league's top-ranked defense. The ground game adds little. The work is split three ways among Etienne, Miller and Kamara, the team averages 3.22 yards a carry, and runners get only 2.11 yards before contact. The one thing the run game does well is short yardage. A 3rd-ranked short-yardage conversion rate supports a staff that has gone for it on every fourth-down chance it has rated.

The defense is the bigger story, because it's new. Last year's unit allowed -0.048 EPA, 10th in the league. This one allows +0.089, 27th, and ranks 31st in both rush EPA allowed and success rate allowed. Some of the 30.2 points allowed per game comes from short fields after turnovers: the four-giveaway Raiders game ended 35-27. That doesn't excuse a group that gives up a 48.3% third-down rate, generates pressure on only 17% of dropbacks and missed enough tackles to rank 25th. Atlanta ran for 205 yards in a 45-24 loss that was all defense. Now LB Kaden Elliss (100% of snaps) and DTs Nathan Shepherd and Vernon Broughton are listed out, which removes the middle of the run defense.

Going forward, the turnover rate should come down, because few offenses keep giving it away at more than two a game. That alone makes them more competitive than 1-4 suggests. The defensive drop looks more structural, and it won't improve until the front is healthy. Expect a team that loses fewer games by blowout and still finishes well short of .500.

strengths.title: Passing game with a real ceiling
strengths.body: When protection holds and the ball stays secure, Shough moves the offense. He threw for 410 yards in Detroit and +10.9 pass EPA in the win at Baltimore, and the overall success rate is a league-average 43.6%. Chris Olave's 54 targets give the offense a clear focal point. The ceiling is real, but consistency is the open question.

strengths.title: Short-yardage and fourth-down aggression
strengths.body: The line converts in short yardage at the 3rd-best rate in the league and rarely gets stuffed. The staff leans into that by going for it on every rated fourth down. That is a sustainable edge that adds possessions, though it also turns failed tries into short fields for the opponent.

concerns.title: Giveaways are wrecking the scoreboard
concerns.body: Eleven turnovers against five takeaways explains much of the -6.6 point differential. It also inflates points allowed through short fields. Turnover rates this extreme usually regress, so expect improvement, but three multi-giveaway games in five means ball security is a real issue, not just bad bounces.

concerns.title: Run defense has collapsed
concerns.body: The defense ranks 31st in both rush EPA allowed and success rate allowed. It also gets off the field on third down less often than almost anyone. This is a sharp break from last year's top-10 unit, and with Elliss and two rotation DTs listed out it is likely to get worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: No pass rush to cover for it
concerns.body: A 17% pressure rate and a 25th-ranked QB hit rate mean opponents get comfortable when they do throw. Combined with the run defense, offenses face little resistance on either kind of play.

trend.note: After a 1-1 start that included a near-miss in Detroit and a win in Baltimore, the Saints have lost three straight. They gave up 35 and 45 at home, then managed just 96 passing yards against Minnesota.

nextGame.headline: Clean pocket for Shough, but a depleted front faces a run-first opponent
nextGame.body:
The Giants are 3-1-1, but their 24th-ranked net EPA is barely better than New Orleans' 27th. The record leans on a 0.833 one-score win rate, +1.44 wins over expectation and special teams that rank 3rd. On paper the matchup suits Shough: New York generates pressure on only 11% of dropbacks, worst in the league, and has allowed WR1s 5 PPR points over their average. The catch is that the Giants rank 2nd in deep-pass EPA allowed, so the production should come underneath and intermediate rather than over the top. On the other side, New York runs far more than the situations suggest (pass rate over expected -9.1, 30th) and controls the clock. That plays straight into the Saints' worst defensive weakness, though the Giants' own run game has been poor at -0.201 EPA per carry.

Availability tilts the wrong way for New Orleans. Elliss, Shepherd, Broughton and Jennings are all listed out, and G Jeremiah Wright is out on the offensive side. The Giants lost DE Chauncey Golston to IR, which weakens an already weak rush. They are also thin at safety: Pinnock is out and Nubin is questionable, along with CB Hood. RT Jermaine Eluemunor (90% snaps) is questionable too. The line of NYG -1.5 looks about right, since the Giants' small efficiency edge and home field roughly offset their luck-driven record.

keyMatchups.title: Shough vs. the league's weakest rush
keyMatchups.body: New York's 11% pressure rate is last in the league, and losing Golston thins it further. Shough should have time, which tends to reduce sacks and forced throws, the main sources of his turnovers. A banged-up Giants secondary adds to the opening.

keyMatchups.title: Giants ground game vs. gutted front
keyMatchups.body: The Giants run heavily and hold the ball 34 minutes a game. The Saints' run defense ranks 31st and is missing its every-down linebacker and two interior linemen. New York's own run efficiency is poor, but this is the defense most likely to make it look competent.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams gap
keyMatchups.body: New York's special teams add 4.37 EPA a game, while the Saints' units are negative. In a game priced under a field goal, a hidden-yardage edge that size can decide the outcome.

nextGame.watch: Whether Shough keeps the ball out of harm's way with a clean pocket. A zero-giveaway game is how New Orleans wins this. Two or more and it doesn't.

restOfSeason.body:
The remaining schedule is mostly middling teams in the 3-2 range, plus four games against Tampa Bay and Arizona, each 1-4. Those give the Saints a realistic path to a few more wins. Turnovers should regress toward normal, which will tighten the point differential and keep them in more games. The defense is the bigger question. Getting the front seven healthy should restore some of last year's competence, but ranking 31st in run success allowed is too far gone to blame on injuries alone.

The passing game is the sustainable part. It should stay around league average, and Jordyn Tyson's return from IR around early November adds another option. The run game will probably stay below average given the poor yards before contact and the three-way split at running back. The likely result is a team that scores enough to stay competitive and allows too much to win often: a 5-or-6-win finish, with the NFC South's overall weakness the only thing keeping the outlook from being worse.
swingFactors: Health of Elliss and the interior DL
Results in four games vs TB and ARI

bets.reason: New York leans on the run more than almost anyone (pass rate over expected -9.1, 30th). The Saints rank 31st in rush EPA allowed and are missing Elliss plus two DTs, and they just gave up 205 rushing yards to Atlanta and 153 to Minnesota.

Olave averages nearly 11 targets a game and faces a defense with the league's worst pressure rate, a thin safety group, and a 5-point PPR surplus allowed to WR1s. The Giants' 2nd-ranked deep-pass defense caps the upside, so this is a modest edge.

confidence.note: Five-game sample, an extreme turnover rate that should regress, and several defensive starters listed out this week
